Meta and Apple have spent recent months going back and forth over how Apple should implement the EU-mandated third-party device pairing mechanism, as detailed below.

Meta and Apple disagree on a feasible approach to EU interoperability

Under Europe's Digital Markets Act, Apple is required to let third-party devices access certain iPhone and iPad features that are currently more tightly integrated with its own accessories.

These include pairing and connectivity functions, aimed at giving competing products the same level of access as accessories such as AirPods and Apple Watch.

For example, Apple has already rolled out a proximity-triggered pairing feature in the EU via iOS 26.5, which lets compatible third-party accessories bring up a simplified pairing prompt when held near an iPhone.

However, Meta's request involves a different capability Apple has yet to ship: allowing an accessory already paired with one iPhone or iPad to automatically work across a user's other iPhones and iPads — similar to how AirPods pairing syncs across Apple devices.

According to findings by Aaron Perris, Apple and Meta have been going back and forth since October 2025, when Meta first filed an interoperability request for the feature.

Based on correspondence published on Apple's EU Interoperability portal, Meta wants its Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses and Quest headsets, once paired with an iPhone or iPad, to automatically work on a user's other iPhones and iPads.

Meta's side of the story is as follows:

Apple's initial response was to propose a set of new APIs that would let third-party apps sync the information needed to reuse accessory pairing data across a user's other iPhones and iPads. Meta said the proposal delivers the core functionality it asked for, but objected to Apple tying API access to the AccessorySetupKit framework, arguing that doing so could disrupt its existing pairing experience outside the EU.

In subsequent exchanges, Apple said it had carefully reviewed Meta's concerns but still intended to proceed with its proposal, noting that Meta had already acknowledged the approach delivers the core functionality it requested.

Apple also pointed out that other developers using AccessorySetupKit outside the EU had not encountered the issues Meta raised.

Meta then reiterated that Apple's approach could harm its device setup experience outside the EU, further clarifying its technical concerns, and again urged Apple to reconsider how the feature is implemented.
